original_question: Let T102(a,b) denote the number of tilings of the (a,b)-benzel in which right stones are allowed, left stones are forbidden, and exactly two of the three bone orientations are allowed. Is it true that for all k >= 0 and n >= 1, except (k,n) = (0,1), one has T102(n+3k, 2n+3k-1) = product_{i=1}^k ((2i)! (2i+2n-2)!)/((i+n-1)! (i+n+k-1)!)?
target_in_paper: Section 5, Problem 5 (“Right stones, two kinds of bones”). ([samuelfhopkins.com](https://www.samuelfhopkins.com/OPAC/files/proceedings/propp.pdf))
correct_elements: Your draft already matches the paper’s official formulation almost verbatim: it uses the correct counting function T_{102}(a,b), the correct tile-set condition (right stones allowed, left stones forbidden, exactly two bone prototiles allowed), the exact parameter family (a,b)=(n+3k,2n+3k−1), the correct product formula, and the same quantifiers and exceptional pair (k,n)=(0,1). ([samuelfhopkins.com](https://www.samuelfhopkins.com/OPAC/files/proceedings/propp.pdf))
missing_details: The draft does not define the (a,b)-benzel itself or state the paper’s admissible parameter range 2≤a≤2b and 2≤b≤2a. ([samuelfhopkins.com](https://www.samuelfhopkins.com/OPAC/files/proceedings/propp.pdf))

It does not make explicit that the five prototiles in the paper are the right stone, the left stone, and the three bones (vertical, rising, and falling). ([samuelfhopkins.com](https://www.samuelfhopkins.com/OPAC/files/proceedings/propp.pdf))

It leaves implicit why T_{102} is well-defined without specifying which two bones are allowed: Section 1 explains that, by threefold rotational symmetry, the count depends only on how many bone prototiles are allowed, not on which pair is chosen. ([samuelfhopkins.com](https://www.samuelfhopkins.com/OPAC/files/proceedings/propp.pdf))

It does not explain that the excluded pair (k,n)=(0,1) corresponds to (a,b)=(1,1), which lies outside the benzel parameter range used in the paper. This follows from the Section 1 definition together with the Problem 5 parameterization. ([samuelfhopkins.com](https://www.samuelfhopkins.com/OPAC/files/proceedings/propp.pdf))

It omits the nearby symmetry relation T_{ijk}(a,b)=T_{ijk}(b,a), which is part of the surrounding context in Section 1 even though it is not part of the formal statement of Problem 5 itself. ([samuelfhopkins.com](https://www.samuelfhopkins.com/OPAC/files/proceedings/propp.pdf))

Ambient ring/field, homogeneity, degree restrictions, and nilpotency conditions are not applicable here, because this is a finite tiling-enumeration problem rather than an algebraic one. ([samuelfhopkins.com](https://www.samuelfhopkins.com/OPAC/files/proceedings/propp.pdf))
refined_question: For integers a,b with 2≤a≤2b and 2≤b≤2a, let the (a,b)-benzel be Propp’s hexagonal-grid region consisting of the unit hexagonal cells lying fully inside the hexagon with vertices a+b, -aω^2-b, aω^2+bω, -a-bω, a+bω^2, and -aω-bω^2, where ω=e^(2πi/3). Let T_{102}(a,b) denote the number of tilings of this region by the right stone together with any two of the three bone prototiles (vertical, rising, and falling), with the left stone forbidden; by the threefold rotational symmetry discussed in Section 1, this number does not depend on which two bone prototiles are chosen. Is it true that for all integers k≥0 and n≥1, except (k,n)=(0,1), one has T_{102}(n+3k,2n+3k-1)=∏_{i=1}^k ((2i)!(2i+2n-2)!)/((i+n-1)!(i+n+k-1)!)? ([samuelfhopkins.com](https://www.samuelfhopkins.com/OPAC/files/proceedings/propp.pdf))
justification: This draft clearly targets Problem 5 and not a neighboring problem: the notation T_{102}, the tile restrictions, the parameter family, and the factorial-product formula coincide with the official statement in Section 5. The only paper-critical material missing from the draft comes from Section 1, which supplies the benzel definition, the meaning of T_{ijk}(a,b), and the rotational-symmetry fact that makes “exactly two bones allowed” a well-defined case. This paper is organized around numbered Problems rather than around a Conjecture 1.1 / Proposition 1.2 / Theorem 1.3 sequence, and the nearest official formulation is therefore Problem 5 itself. ([samuelfhopkins.com](https://www.samuelfhopkins.com/OPAC/files/proceedings/propp.pdf))
